html:
The Rattanakosin Kingdom was Siam, today's Thailand, from 1782 to 1932, ruled from Bangkok by the Chakri dynasty. Rama I founded it after the fall of Ayutthaya to Burma in 1767 (Sukhothai and Ayutthaya) and the short reign of King Taksin. He moved the capital across the river to Bangkok and built the Grand Palace and the temple of the Emerald Buddha, Wat Phra Kaew.

Siam ruled as the centre of a ring of lesser rulers who paid it tribute: Lan Na, the Lao kingdoms, Cambodia and several Malay sultanates. In 1805 it gathered its laws into the Three Seals Law. It fought Burma and crushed a revolt from Vientiane in 1827 and 1828.

In the 1800s two kings steered Siam through the age of empires:

  • Mongkut, Rama IV, a former monk and scholar, signed the Bowring Treaty with Britain in 1855, opening the country to trade.
  • Chulalongkorn, Rama V, who reigned from 1868 to 1910, set up modern ministries, schools and railways and abolished slavery.

Siam gave up Lao lands and Cambodian provinces to France and its northern Malay states to Britain, but it kept its independence, the only country in Southeast Asia never colonised. The Siamese revolution of 1932 ended absolute monarchy. The story continues in Siam, then Thailand.
